# Three Roles, Not Three Arbitrary Percentages

A train--validation--test design separates model construction from performance
assessment:

- the **training set** estimates parameters for a candidate procedure;
- the **validation set** chooses features, transformations, hyperparameters,
  thresholds, or candidate procedures; and
- the **test set** is opened once to estimate the performance of the locked
  procedure on new independent units.

The labels describe information flow, not fixed percentages. A 60/20/20 random
split is not automatically sound, and cross-validation can replace a single
validation split within the development data. What matters is that the test data
do not influence development and that the split represents the intended future
use.

```text
Development data                         Locked test data
  training <-> validation                    |
  fit, tune, revise, debug                    v
  lock the complete procedure  ------>  one final assessment
```

Once test results guide a new feature, threshold, subgroup definition, or model,
the test set has become validation data. The revised procedure needs another
untouched assessment.

# Define the Prediction Estimand First

Let $A$ denote the locked learning algorithm, $D_{\mathrm{dev}}$ the development
sample, and

$$
\hat f=A(D_{\mathrm{dev}}).
$$

For a future population $P_\star$, the conditional test-risk target for this fitted
model is

$$
R_\star(\hat f)=
\operatorname E_{(X,Y)\sim P_\star}
\left[L\{Y,\hat f(X)\}\mid D_{\mathrm{dev}}\right].
$$

If an independent test set of $n_{\mathrm{test}}$ units is sampled from
$P_\star$, its empirical loss is

$$
\widehat R_{\mathrm{test}}
=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{test}}}L\{Y_i,\hat f(X_i)\}.
$$

This interpretation requires independent test units, a prespecified analysis,
and alignment between the test distribution and $P_\star$. If test cases come
from the same laboratory and period as training cases, the estimate does not by
itself establish performance in a new hospital, ancestry group, instrument, or
future time period.

The target also determines the metric. Probability prediction calls for proper
scores and calibration; ranking calls for a discrimination metric; a clinical
decision requires a loss or utility tied to consequences. Reporting only the
best-looking metric after seeing the test data creates another selection problem.

# Design the Split Around the Experimental Unit

The independent unit of inference and deployment must be assigned wholly to one
partition. The row of an analysis table is not necessarily that unit.

In high-throughput biology:

- reads and technical lanes belong to a library;
- cells may belong to a donor or independently randomized specimen;
- repeated visits and images belong to a participant;
- aliquots and assay replicates belong to a biological sample;
- related participants may belong to a family cluster.

Putting correlated observations from one unit on both sides of a split leaks
unit-specific information. It also makes precision appear to depend on the number
of cells or reads rather than the number of independently sampled donors or
specimens.

## Random, grouped, temporal, and external splits

| Intended claim | Appropriate assessment design | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| New exchangeable unit from the same setting | random unit-level split | does not test site or time shift |
| New unit from a represented cluster | grouped split by unit, family, or specimen | clusters may still resemble one another |
| Future cases | chronological split with training before testing | time and protocol changes are combined |
| New site, laboratory, or platform | leave-site-out or external test cohort | few sites can make results unstable |
| New spatial region | blocked or buffered spatial split | depends on deployment scale |

A harder split is not inherently better. It is better only when it matches the
scientific claim. Random and external-site assessments can both be useful when
they are labeled as different estimands rather than treated as interchangeable
replicates.

# Keep the Test Set Outside Development

Test isolation covers more than outcome labels. The test set should not determine:

- inclusion and exclusion rules invented after inspection;
- normalization, imputation, batch correction, or feature scaling parameters;
- feature filtering, dimension reduction, or representation learning;
- model family, hyperparameters, ensemble weights, or stopping rules;
- decision thresholds, probability calibration, or subgroup definitions;
- which performance metrics and comparisons are emphasized.

Code debugging can also overfit the test set when repeated test evaluation reveals
which changes help. Freeze the data-processing specification and metric definitions
before assessment, keep a development-only debugging dataset, and log every access
to the test outcomes. In a benchmark shared with many analysts, repeated community
use can exhaust the effective independence of the benchmark even if each submission
sees only a score.

Training and test transformations must also reflect deployment. It can be valid
to apply externally fixed constants or reference panels to every partition. By
contrast, estimating a global mean, principal-component basis, gene signature,
or calibration curve from all partitions lets test information shape the model.

# Allocate Information According to the Goal

There is no universally optimal split fraction. More development units improve
fitting and tuning; more test units reduce uncertainty in performance. The useful
sample size is the number of independent units and informative outcomes, not the
number of measured variables or technical observations.

Before splitting, plan the precision of the primary test metric. For a mean test
loss with independent unit-level losses $\ell_i$, a basic standard error is

$$
\operatorname{SE}(\bar\ell)
=\frac{s_\ell}{\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{test}}}},
$$

where $s_\ell$ is the sample standard deviation of the unit-level losses. Clustered
test data require cluster-aware uncertainty. Accuracy has binomial uncertainty
only under restrictive independent, identically distributed classification
conditions; area under the curve, calibration measures, and threshold-selected
metrics need their own methods.

Rare outcomes, small subgroups, and site-level claims can require a test set much
larger than a rule-of-thumb percentage suggests. When data are limited, nested
[cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd) can use development data efficiently and
estimate the entire tuning procedure. It does not eliminate the value of later
external validation under the real deployment distribution.

# Validation Is a Development Activity

The validation set answers questions such as which penalty, feature set, or
threshold to use. Because the chosen candidate is the winner among noisy validation
estimates, its validation performance is optimistic. This is the same selection
mechanism behind the winner's curse.

The final test evaluates the complete rule that made those choices. If model
selection uses five-fold CV, preprocessing and tuning occur within that CV. If
many modeling strategies are compared, the test evaluates the winning strategy
only after the comparison is finished. Reporting uncertainty for the fitted
coefficients does not account for all uncertainty introduced by this adaptive
development path.

A model registry or analysis record should preserve the training-data version,
code version, random seeds, feature definitions, hyperparameters, preprocessing
objects, threshold, and primary metrics. Reproducibility of the locked artifact is
part of statistical validity.

# Worked Multi-site Omics Example

Suppose 300 donors from four hospitals have plasma proteomics measurements and a
binary one-year outcome. The intended tool will be deployed prospectively at
hospitals not involved in development.

A random donor-level test split estimates performance for new donors mixed across
the four familiar hospitals. It does not estimate new-hospital performance. A
stronger design reserves one or more hospitals as an external test and uses only
the remaining hospitals for feature filtering, missing-value handling, tuning,
threshold choice, and calibration. If only four hospitals exist, site-level
uncertainty remains large; hundreds of donors cannot replace independent site
replication.

All aliquots and technical repeats from one donor remain in the same partition.
When the locked model is evaluated, report the prespecified proper score,
discrimination, calibration intercept and slope, clinically relevant threshold
performance, and intervals based on donors or sites as appropriate. Examine
performance by site and scientifically important groups without selecting only
favorable subgroups.

Statistically, the test estimates performance for the sampled sites, protocol,
case mix, prevalence, and follow-up process. Biologically, a protein signature
that predicts outcome may reflect disease mechanism, treatment allocation,
comorbidity, handling time, or batch. Mechanistic interpretation requires separate
design and evidence.

# Distribution Shift and Post-deployment Monitoring

An independent test set can be internally honest yet externally irrelevant.
Transport can fail through changes in covariates, outcome prevalence, the
conditional relationship $P(Y\mid X)$, measurement, missingness, or clinical
actions triggered by predictions.

Before deployment, compare population definitions, covariate support, assay
protocols, site and time composition, missingness, and outcome ascertainment.
Report where extrapolation occurs. Recalibration may repair a changed intercept or
scale but cannot generally fix missing predictors, altered labels, or a changed
biological mechanism.

After deployment, monitor data quality, missingness, calibration, performance by
relevant groups, and operational consequences. A performance drop is evidence to
investigate; it does not uniquely identify whether the cause is biological drift,
measurement change, workflow change, or sampling error. Updating the model starts
a new development cycle and requires a new assessment plan.

# A Design and Reporting Checklist

1. State the future population, prediction unit, horizon, outcome, and primary
   loss before splitting.
2. Identify biological and technical replication; assign every correlated unit
   to exactly one partition.
3. Choose random, grouped, temporal, spatial, or site-based separation to match
   the intended claim.
4. Keep preprocessing, selection, tuning, calibration, and threshold choice
   inside development data.
5. Lock the pipeline, test analysis, and reporting metrics before opening test
   outcomes.
6. Report uncertainty at the independent-unit level and show clinically or
   biologically relevant subgroup results without post hoc cherry-picking.
7. Distinguish internal performance, external transport, statistical prediction,
   and biological mechanism.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd) explains fold-based performance
  estimation and nested tuning within development data.
- [Selection bias and winner's curse](../statistical-inference/selection-bias-and-winners-curse.qmd)
  explains why reused validation results are optimistic.
- [Variable selection and nested-model testing](variable-selection-and-nested-model-testing.qmd)
  describes adaptive model search and its inferential cost.
- [Odds ratios, probabilities, and calibration](odds-ratios-probabilities-and-calibration.qmd)
  distinguishes discrimination from reliable predicted probabilities.
- [Sensitivity analysis and robustness](../statistical-inference/sensitivity-analysis-and-robustness.qmd)
  provides a framework for conclusions that depend on design choices.

The test set is an independent scientific assessment, not a final source of model
ideas. Its credibility comes from a locked pipeline, experimental-unit-aware
separation, a prespecified estimand and metric, and correspondence to deployment.
Technical replication improves measurement but cannot substitute for independent
donors, specimens, sites, or future periods. When the deployment distribution
changes, transparent external validation and monitoring matter more than a
favorable internal split.
